promptText: In the Next.js App Router, how is a route's rendering mode (static vs dynamic) actually determined?
options: It's derived from what the route touches — reading cookies()/headers()/searchParams or using an uncached fetch forces dynamic rendering; otherwise the route is rendered statically
You must explicitly toggle a single global "SSR mode" setting in next.config.js for the whole app
Every route in the App Router is always rendered dynamically on every request by design
Rendering mode is chosen automatically based on how many components the route imports
explanation: In the App Router, rendering mode emerges from data access rather than an explicit toggle — request-scoped reads or uncached fetches flip a route to dynamic, while a route with only cacheable fetches stays static (SSG/ISR).

promptText: Why does calling new Date().toLocaleTimeString() directly during a component's render commonly cause a hydration mismatch?
options: The server computes the value at build/request time and the client computes it again during hydration moments later, producing two different strings that don't match
toLocaleTimeString() is not a valid function to call inside a React component
Hydration always fails whenever any component uses the Date object at all, regardless of how it's used
The server never executes component render functions, so the value is always undefined server-side
explanation: Hydration requires the client's first render to produce the exact same output the server sent; a value like the current time changes between the server's render and the client's re-render moments later, so React detects a mismatch.

promptText: What is the defining difference between a React Server Component and a Client Component in the Next.js App Router?
options: A Server Component never ships its JavaScript to the browser at all; a Client Component's code is bundled and sent to run in the browser
Server Components can use useState and useEffect, but Client Components cannot
Client Components can directly query a database, while Server Components cannot
Server Components run only in the browser, after hydration completes
explanation: The core distinction is the bundle and execution boundary: Server Components render only on the server and their code/dependencies never reach the client bundle, while Client Components (marked "use client") ship their JS to run and hydrate in the browser.

promptText: Why might importing a Node-only database driver into code running on the Edge runtime fail?
options: The Edge runtime only supports Web-standard APIs (fetch, Web Crypto, streams) and has no access to Node-specific modules like fs or native addons
The Edge runtime forbids any code that reads environment variables
Node database drivers are always synchronous, which the Edge runtime doesn't allow
The Edge runtime requires all imports to be written in TypeScript
explanation: The Edge runtime is a lightweight, Web-API-only environment; it lacks full Node compatibility (no fs, no native addons), so importing a Node-only driver into Edge code typically produces a build or runtime error.

promptText: Why must a Server Action independently re-authenticate and re-authorize its caller, even though it's only invoked from your own app's form?
options: Next generates a real network-callable endpoint for every Server Action, so anyone who can construct the right request can call it directly, regardless of which UI it was originally wired to
Server Actions run entirely inside the browser, so there's no server-side session to check
Server Actions automatically inherit whatever validation the client-side form already performed
Authentication is handled entirely by the "use server" directive itself, with no extra code needed
explanation: A Server Action is effectively a public POST endpoint Next.js generates automatically — it must validate input and check auth/ownership exactly like any REST or GraphQL endpoint, since it can be invoked directly, not only through the intended UI.

promptText: Why does forgetting the priority prop on a hero image commonly hurt a page's LCP score?
options: Without priority, the image lazy-loads like an off-screen image instead of being preloaded, delaying when the Largest Contentful Paint element finishes rendering
Images without priority are served in a lower-resolution format regardless of viewport size
priority is required for next/image to generate a srcset at all
Missing priority causes the image to be excluded from the production build entirely
explanation: next/image lazy-loads by default; marking the above-the-fold LCP image with priority makes it preload immediately instead of waiting its turn, which directly helps Largest Contentful Paint timing.

promptText: A layout and its page both call the same fetch-wrapped function to get the current user during one render. Why does this typically result in only one network request?
options: Request memoization automatically dedupes identical fetch calls (same URL and options) made during a single render pass, regardless of how many components call it
The Data Cache persists the result across every future request indefinitely, so only the very first visitor to the site ever triggers a real fetch
Next.js only allows one fetch call per route by design, throwing an error on any second attempt
The layout and the page are always merged into a single component before rendering
explanation: Request memoization dedupes identical fetch calls made during a single server render pass and is automatic for fetch (and for functions wrapped in React's cache()) — it's distinct from and shorter-lived than the persistent, opt-in Data Cache.

promptText: A product's data appears on its own detail page, the homepage's "featured products" section, and a search index page. Which invalidation approach lets you refresh all of these at once after an edit?
options: Tag every fetch for that product's data with a shared tag (e.g. via next: { tags }) and call revalidateTag, which invalidates every cached entry carrying that tag anywhere in the app
Call revalidatePath on the product detail page only, since Next automatically propagates invalidation to any other page referencing the same entity
revalidatePath and revalidateTag are interchangeable and always invalidate the exact same scope
Restart the Next.js server process, since that is the only way to clear cached data spanning multiple routes
explanation: revalidatePath only reaches one route's cache; revalidateTag invalidates every cached fetch anywhere in the app that was tagged with that value, which is exactly what's needed when the same data appears across multiple, otherwise-unrelated routes.

promptText: A server component fetches an ORM model instance and passes it directly as a prop into a client component. What problem does this risk, and why?
options: Props crossing the server-to-client boundary are serialized into the RSC payload; an ORM instance's prototype methods don't survive that serialization, so the client ends up with only its plain enumerable data fields (or an outright error), losing expected behavior
Client components can only ever receive props whose values are functions, so an object like this is rejected immediately
ORM instances are automatically converted into React elements before crossing the boundary
Passing an ORM instance always throws a hydration mismatch error, unrelated to serialization
explanation: Server-to-client props are serialized into the RSC payload and reconstructed on the client, not passed by live reference — a class instance's prototype chain and methods don't survive that round-trip, so the fix is stripping to a plain object (a DTO) before crossing the boundary.

promptText: In a tree where an outer Suspense wraps Header, an inner Suspense (around just Reviews), and Footer, what happens if Header itself suspends?
options: Because Header has no Suspense boundary of its own, its suspension propagates up to the outer boundary, replacing the entire subtree — including the otherwise-fine Reviews and Footer — with the outer fallback
Only Header's own content disappears; Reviews and Footer continue rendering normally regardless
React throws a build error because a component cannot suspend unless it is the direct child of its own dedicated boundary
The inner Suspense boundary automatically absorbs Header's suspension since it appears later in the tree
explanation: When a component suspends, React shows the fallback of the nearest enclosing Suspense boundary; since Header isn't individually wrapped, its suspension bubbles to the outer boundary and replaces the whole subtree with that boundary's fallback, not just Header's own output.

promptText: Why is it considered a mistake to implement full authorization logic (e.g. checking database-backed permissions) directly inside Next.js middleware?
options: Middleware runs on the Edge runtime with a tight CPU/size budget on every matched request, so it's meant for cheap gatekeeping (token presence checks, redirects) — full DB-backed authorization belongs in a server component or route handler running on Node
Middleware cannot read cookies or headers at all, making authorization checks technically impossible there
Middleware only executes after a page has already fully rendered, so a failed authorization check there can't prevent content from being shown
Next.js limits every app to zero middleware files, so authorization logic has nowhere else reasonable to live
explanation: Middleware is a fast Edge gatekeeper, not an auth server — it runs on every matched request with Web-API-only constraints and a tight budget, so the pattern is a cheap presence/validity check there and real, database-backed authorization downstream on Node.

promptText: What problem does Partial Prerendering (PPR) solve that plain per-route static/dynamic classification could not?
options: Before PPR, a single dynamic read (like cookies()) anywhere in a route forced the entire route to render dynamically on every request, even if most of the page was static; PPR lets a static shell serve instantly while only the Suspense-wrapped dynamic parts render per-request
PPR eliminates the need for any caching layer in Next.js entirely, replacing both the Data Cache and Full Route Cache
PPR allows a route to be statically rendered even when the page never calls generateStaticParams
PPR removes the requirement for a Suspense boundary around any asynchronous data fetching
explanation: PPR resolves the all-or-nothing static/dynamic decision at the granularity of individual Suspense boundaries instead of the whole route, so a mostly-static page with one personalized widget can prerender the shell and stream only the dynamic hole.

promptText: A route is set to export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic', but one of its fetch calls uses { next: { revalidate: 3600 } }. What actually happens on each request?
options: The route itself is fully re-rendered on every request since the Full Route Cache doesn't apply to it, but that specific fetch's result can still be served from the Data Cache for up to an hour — the two caching layers are independently controlled
force-dynamic overrides all caching everywhere in the route, so the tagged fetch is also refetched from the origin on every single request
The revalidate option on the fetch call silently forces the entire route back into the Full Route Cache, contradicting force-dynamic
Next.js throws a build error because dynamic routes are not permitted to use any fetch caching options
explanation: The Full Route Cache and the Data Cache are separate, independently controllable layers: going dynamic disables the Full Route Cache for that route, but individual fetches inside it can still opt into the Data Cache, which is exactly how an otherwise-dynamic page keeps one expensive-but-stable sub-fetch fast.

promptText: A Stripe webhook Route Handler calls await request.json() first, then tries to verify the payload's signature against JSON.stringify() of that parsed object. Verification keeps failing even for genuine Stripe requests. What is the root cause and fix?
options: Signature verification is computed over the exact raw bytes Stripe sent; re-serializing a parsed-then-stringified object can differ in whitespace or key order from the original, so the fix is to read the raw body via request.text() and verify against that exact string before parsing it
Stripe webhooks cannot be verified inside Next.js Route Handlers at all; verification must happen in a separate microservice
The handler is missing an OPTIONS export, which is required before any POST request's signature can be validated
Signature verification only works when the route runs on the Edge runtime, not the Node runtime
explanation: A webhook's signature is computed over the literal bytes sent, so calling request.json() first and re-stringifying loses byte-for-byte fidelity (whitespace, key order); the fix is reading the raw body via request.text() and verifying against that exact string before parsing.

promptText: A 'like' button calls await likePost(postId) (a Server Action) and only updates its UI after the promise resolves. How does this affect INP, and what change fixes it without abandoning Server Actions?
options: The visual update is blocked on a full network round trip, directly adding that latency to the interaction's perceived responsiveness; wrapping the state update in useOptimistic and firing the action inside useTransition lets the UI paint immediately while the action resolves in the background
INP is a purely server-side metric, so nothing about client-side button behavior can affect it
Server Actions are always synchronous, so no network latency is ever involved when they're called from an onClick handler
The fix is to convert the Server Action into a Client Component so it runs entirely in the browser instead
explanation: INP measures the delay between an interaction and the next visual update; naively awaiting a Server Action before updating state makes the network round trip part of that delay, while useOptimistic plus useTransition lets the UI paint on the next frame and reconciles with the real result once the action resolves.
